meta.label: Browsers
meta.attribution: Built from browser makers' own privacy and telemetry documentation, licence agreements, source repositories, regulator and government records, independent security research, app-store and package-registry listings, community wikis, press reports and browser download pages, not measured data. Browser settings and defaults change between releases, so check current documentation before relying on any of these. Privacy reflects default tracking and fingerprinting protection, not what a setting can be turned up to; openness reflects whether the browser's own code, not just the rendering engine underneath it, is published and under what licence; respect reflects the maker's business model and any regulatory findings about market power over the browser; accessibility covers both how easy the browser is to start using and how compatible it is with ordinary sites and existing extensions. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare browsers by privacy, everyday access, openness, and data portability.

criteria.label: Easy to start and compatible with sites

products.name: Tor Browser

privacy.note: Tor Project says Tor Browser isolates each site visited so third-party trackers and ads cannot follow you, and prevents someone watching your connection from knowing what sites you visit.

openness.note: Tor Project distributes Tor Browser as open-source privacy software.

portability.note: Tor Browser is a standards-based Firefox derivative available across major desktop and mobile platforms, so switching devices does not require a different browser.

respect.note: The Tor Project describes itself as a US 501(c)(3) nonprofit, founded in 2006 to maintain Tor's development, with no advertising business tied to the browser.

accessibility.note: Tor Browser is a free download for major platforms, but routing all traffic through Tor is markedly slower than an ordinary browser and some sites block or challenge Tor traffic.

economical.note: Tor Browser is free to download and use.

products.description: The strongest anti-tracking, anti-surveillance browser here, free and open source, built and maintained by a nonprofit. Routing everything through Tor makes ordinary browsing noticeably slower and some sites harder to reach.

products.name: Firefox

privacy.note: Mozilla's 2019 rollout announcement says Enhanced Tracking Protection is on by default for new users as part of the Standard setting, blocking known third-party tracking cookies.

openness.note: GitHub describes mozilla-firefox/firefox as the official repository of Mozilla's Firefox web browser, published for public inspection.

portability.note: Firefox is a cross-platform browser built on open web standards, with ordinary bookmark, password and history export tools.

respect.note: Firefox's own privacy page says Mozilla does not sell what little it knows about users, but Mozilla's 2024 annual report states the majority of its revenue still comes from commercial search partnerships, the kind of deal that keeps a default search engine in front of every Firefox user.

accessibility.note: Firefox is a mature, free, cross-platform browser with broad site compatibility and an established extension ecosystem.

economical.note: Firefox's download and marketing pages list no purchase price for the browser.

products.description: An open-source browser with tracker blocking on by default and broad compatibility. Mozilla says it does not sell user data, but its own annual report says most of its revenue still comes from commercial search deals.

products.name: Brave

privacy.note: Brave says Shields block trackers, cross-site cookies, phishing and fingerprinting by default, with no extra downloads or settings needed.

openness.note: Brave's browser source is public on GitHub, built on Chromium and licensed under MPL-2.0.

portability.note: Brave is Chromium-based, so extensions and browser data behave much like Chrome's, making migration in either direction straightforward.

respect.note: Default tracker blocking is respectful of a visitor's attention, but Brave's own optional Brave Rewards/Ads system keeps an advertising layer inside the same product.

accessibility.note: Brave looks and behaves like Chrome, supports Chrome extensions, and is free to install, which makes switching to it low-friction.

economical.note: Brave is free to download and use.

products.description: A Chromium browser with strong tracker blocking on by default and a public source repository. Its own optional ads and rewards system is a reminder that advertising is still part of the product.

products.name: Safari

privacy.note: Apple says Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention uses on-device machine learning to fight cross-site tracking, including hiding a user's IP address from trackers.

openness.note: Safari itself is closed Apple software, though the underlying WebKit engine is described as a fast, open-source web browser engine.

portability.note: Safari syncs passwords, bookmarks, history and tabs across Mac, iPad, iPhone and Apple Watch, but there is no current Safari for Windows, Android or Linux, so switching away from Apple devices means switching browsers too.

respect.note: The European Commission's Digital Markets Act gatekeepers portal lists Safari as one of Apple's designated core platform services, meaning EU regulators judged it to have gatekeeper-level market power over how people browse on Apple devices.

accessibility.note: Safari comes preinstalled on every Mac, iPhone and iPad and is tightly integrated with those devices, which makes it the effortless default for Apple users and unavailable to everyone else.

economical.note: Safari is included at no extra cost on Apple devices.

products.description: Apple's default browser, with real on-device tracking prevention and deep integration on Apple hardware. It is closed, does not exist for Windows, Android or Linux, and is one of the EU's designated DMA gatekeeper services.

products.name: Google Chrome

privacy.note: Google's privacy policy says information collected includes Chrome browsing history synced with a Google Account, along with identifiers that persist a user's activity across sessions.

openness.note: The underlying Chromium project describes itself as open source, but Google Chrome adds proprietary Google components on top of it and is not itself published as open source.

portability.note: Chrome supports ordinary bookmark and password export and runs on nearly every platform, though signing in with a Google Account ties browsing history to that account.

respect.note: The European Commission's Digital Markets Act gatekeepers portal lists Google Chrome as one of Alphabet's designated core platform services, one of 22 services across six companies that EU regulators found to have gatekeeper-level market power.

accessibility.note: Chrome highlights performance features like Energy Saver and Memory Saver, a large extension catalogue, and sign-in sync of bookmarks and passwords across devices.

economical.note: Chrome's download page lists no purchase price; it is offered as a standard free download.

products.description: The dominant browser, free, fast and compatible with nearly everything. It is also the browser the EU has judged to give Google gatekeeper-level market power, and Google's own privacy policy covers synced browsing history and cross-service identifiers.

products.name: Microsoft Edge

privacy.note: Microsoft's own documentation says Edge's Balanced tracking-prevention level, the default, blocks trackers from sites a user has not engaged with and blocks known malicious trackers like fingerprinters and cryptominers, while allowing more tracking than the Strict level.

openness.note: Edge is built on the open-source Chromium project, but Microsoft's own Edge browser layered on top is proprietary.

portability.note: Chromium compatibility and exportable browser data make switching in or out of Edge straightforward, though Windows and Microsoft account integration add some pull to stay.

respect.note: Microsoft's privacy statement covers broad diagnostic, account, browsing and search data collection used for product improvement and personalized advertising, and the European Commission concluded in February 2024 that Edge, unlike Chrome and Safari, should not be designated a Digital Markets Act gatekeeper service.

accessibility.note: Edge is preinstalled on Windows, optimized for it, and bundles free Microsoft 365 web apps alongside the browser.

economical.note: Edge is a free download with no purchase price listed.

products.description: A capable Chromium browser, free and tightly built into Windows, with default tracking prevention that still allows some tracking at its Balanced setting. The EU concluded Edge does not have the market power of Chrome or Safari.

products.name: LibreWolf

privacy.note: LibreWolf says it hardens Firefox against tracking and fingerprinting, removes telemetry and data collection, and ships with uBlock Origin already included.

openness.note: LibreWolf publishes its source and describes itself as a community-driven open-source browser project.

portability.note: LibreWolf stays close to Firefox and can import similar data, but it intentionally disables DRM playback by default and depends on package managers or the user for updates rather than an automatic updater.

respect.note: LibreWolf describes its priorities as privacy, security and user freedom, explicitly over experiments, adware, telemetry or platform-growth features.

accessibility.note: LibreWolf has no built-in auto-update, disables DRM content playback by default, and can break some streaming or DRM-protected sites, trading everyday convenience for hardened defaults.

economical.note: LibreWolf is free to download and use.

products.description: A hardened, open-source Firefox fork that strips telemetry and disables DRM playback by default. Those same defaults mean no automatic updates and some streaming sites will not work without extra setup.

products.name: DuckDuckGo Browser

privacy.note: DuckDuckGo's own tracking-protections documentation lists third-party tracker loading protection, cookie protections, CNAME cloaking protection, fingerprinting defenses and HTTPS upgrading, and says DuckDuckGo never tracks a user's searches.

openness.note: DuckDuckGo publishes its web-tracking protections in detail, but the consumer browser itself is an operated proprietary app rather than a published open-source browser project.

portability.note: The browser is available on Windows, Mac, iOS and Android, but its strongest privacy bundle is specific to DuckDuckGo rather than portable to another browser.

respect.note: DuckDuckGo's browser is built around blocking trackers and ads by default rather than an advertising-and-profiling business inside the browsing experience itself.

accessibility.note: DuckDuckGo markets the browser as a one-download privacy upgrade across major desktop and mobile platforms.

economical.note: DuckDuckGo Browser is free to download and use.

products.description: A mainstream-friendly privacy browser that blocks trackers and ads by default with no configuration needed. It is free and easy to adopt, but it is a closed, DuckDuckGo-operated product rather than an open-source project.

products.name: Opera Browser

privacy.note: Opera advertises an ad blocker and tracking protection built into the browser, and says its free browser VPN neither collects nor stores any data, with the no-log policy independently audited by Deloitte.

openness.note: Opera is a proprietary Chromium-based browser rather than a published open-source browser distribution.

portability.note: Chromium compatibility and Opera Sync make switching in and out manageable, though the built-in VPN, ad blocker and AI features are Opera-specific.

respect.note: Opera's own privacy notice describes collecting technical, usage and marketing data, including through Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity, and the browser markets built-in AI, VPN and account features alongside its privacy tools.

accessibility.note: Opera is a mature, easy-to-install mainstream browser bundling an ad blocker, tracker blocker, free VPN and built-in AI assistant.

economical.note: Opera's browser and its browser-only VPN are free; a separate VPN Pro subscription for device-wide protection costs around four dollars a month.

products.description: A recognizable mainstream browser with a free built-in ad blocker, tracker blocker and VPN. Its own privacy notice also describes broad technical, usage and marketing data collection, so the built-in privacy tools sit alongside an ordinary data-driven business.

products.name: Zen Browser

privacy.note: Zen's own security documentation says online safety and privacy are its top priorities, built on Firefox's tracking-protection and encrypted-connection infrastructure.

openness.note: Zen's desktop repository is public on GitHub, describes itself as open source, and is licensed under MPL-2.0.

portability.note: Zen is Firefox-based and cross-platform, and can sync through Mozilla's own Firefox Sync infrastructure, which Zen says it cannot access.

respect.note: Zen is an open-source, community-run project rather than an advertising or data business layered on top of Firefox.

accessibility.note: Zen is a newer browser with a smaller support ecosystem and less battle-tested compatibility than Firefox or Chrome, though it is free to download.

economical.note: Zen Browser is free to download and use.

products.description: A newer, open-source, Firefox-based browser aimed at Arc-like tab and workspace features without giving up privacy-oriented defaults. It is smaller and less battle-tested than Firefox or Chrome.

products.name: Orion Browser

privacy.note: Kagi says Orion has zero-telemetry browsing with built-in ad blocking and anti-tracking, and no AI data collection.

openness.note: Orion is a proprietary Kagi browser built on WebKit rather than a published open-source browser project.

portability.note: Orion supports Safari, Chrome and Firefox extensions, but is available for macOS, iOS and iPadOS today, with Linux still in beta and Windows still in development, which limits where it can travel with a user.

respect.note: Kagi's privacy documentation says Orion has no built-in telemetry, so it cannot phone home and expose a user's data.

accessibility.note: Orion is strongest for Apple users today; Linux support is in beta and Windows support is still in development, so most people cannot yet use it as their everyday browser.

economical.note: Orion is a free download funded by optional Orion Plus subscriptions or lifetime licenses.

products.description: A zero-telemetry WebKit browser from Kagi that supports Safari, Chrome and Firefox extensions. It is strongest for Apple users today, since Windows support is still in development and Linux is in beta.

products.name: Vivaldi

privacy.note: Vivaldi's browser privacy policy says browsing history, typed search keywords and downloaded content are stored in the user's own client profile, with only a small daily check-in message (device ID, version, CPU architecture, screen resolution) sent to Vivaldi's servers in Iceland.

openness.note: Vivaldi says roughly 92 per cent of the browser's code comes from open-source Chromium, 3 per cent is Vivaldi's own published open-source backend code, and only the remaining 5 per cent, the UI layer, is closed source.

portability.note: Vivaldi supports importing and exporting bookmarks, passwords, history and other browser data from other browsers, making it straightforward to move in or out of.

respect.note: Vivaldi is not built on an ad-network business, and its privacy policy frames data minimization as a core product value rather than a compliance afterthought.

accessibility.note: Vivaldi is a free browser for major desktop and mobile platforms, though its dense, feature-rich interface takes more getting used to than a stripped-down browser.

economical.note: Vivaldi is free to download and use.

products.description: A highly customizable, mostly open-source browser that keeps most personal data on the device and sends only a small daily check-in to Vivaldi's own servers. Only its UI layer, about 5 per cent of the code, stays closed.

products.name: Mullvad Browser

privacy.note: Mullvad Browser is developed together with the Tor Project and designed to minimize tracking and fingerprinting, with telemetry removed rather than collected and later disabled.

openness.note: Mullvad Browser's source is published publicly on GitHub under the Mozilla Public License v2.

portability.note: The browser is available for Windows, macOS and Linux, but there is no mobile version, and it intentionally limits fingerprintable customization rather than offering a full sync ecosystem.

respect.note: Mullvad says it does not earn any money from the browser itself; its income comes from its separate VPN service.

accessibility.note: Mullvad Browser is free for desktop, but privacy-hardened defaults and no mobile version make it a narrower daily driver than mainstream browsers.

economical.note: Mullvad Browser is free to use, with or without a Mullvad VPN subscription.

products.description: A Tor Project and Mullvad collaboration built to reduce tracking and fingerprinting, free and open source, funded by Mullvad's separate VPN business rather than the browser itself. Desktop only, with no mobile version.

products.name: Samsung Internet

privacy.note: Samsung's own newsroom says Samsung Internet's AI-powered Smart Anti-tracking is 'turned on by default', blocking cookies and third parties attempting to track personal information and stopping cross-site trackers from working around tracker blocking. Samsung's current Google Play listing still describes Smart Anti-Tracking as identifying domains with cross-site tracking ability and blocking their cookie access, but does not say whether it ships switched on.

openness.note: Samsung's developer release notes describe each version's web engine as an upgraded Chromium build, and say the browser is distributed through the Samsung Galaxy Store and Google Play, with some versions only preloaded on Galaxy devices. Samsung publishes no source for the browser itself.

portability.note: heise reported in October 2025 that Samsung Internet for PC launched as a beta for Windows 10 and 11, initially only in the USA and South Korea, with bookmarks, history and Samsung Pass logins synced across devices through a Samsung account. There is no Mac, Linux or iOS version.

respect.note: Samsung's Google Play data-safety listing says 'No data shared with third parties', but that the app may collect app activity and device or other IDs, and sync and login features run through a Samsung account.

accessibility.note: Google Play lists Samsung Browser at more than one billion downloads, offered for phones, tablets and Galaxy Watch, and Samsung's release notes say it runs on Android 8.0 and above, not only on Samsung hardware.

economical.note: Samsung Internet is a free download on Google Play and the Galaxy Store.

products.description: The browser preinstalled on Samsung Galaxy phones, with Samsung's Smart Anti-tracking switched on by default. It is a closed Chromium-based app that lives mainly on Android, with a Windows version still rolling out.

products.name: Dia

privacy.note: Dia's plans page lists a 'Built-in ad and tracking blocker' in the free browser, but its privacy policy says The Browser Company collects feature usage data and 'may also collect and use your Content to improve Dia, unless you opt out'.

openness.note: Dia is offered as a proprietary download for macOS and Windows from The Browser Company's site, which publishes no browser source code.

portability.note: Dia is available for macOS and Windows and its site says Sync is end-to-end encrypted, but no Linux or mobile version is offered.

respect.note: Dia's privacy policy says it does not sell, share or process personal data for targeted advertising. Its business is paid AI plans, and Atlassian announced in September 2025 that it had agreed to acquire The Browser Company to make Dia a browser for knowledge work tied to Atlassian's products.

accessibility.note: Dia is a free download for macOS and Windows, with profiles, tab groups and split view in the free plan and AI features behind a 14-day trial and paid plans.

economical.note: Dia's free 'Better Browser' plan includes the browser and its blocker; paid AI plans are listed at 10 to 100 dollars a month, and the FAQ on the same page prices the middle plan at 20.

products.description: The AI-focused browser from the makers of Arc, now owned by Atlassian, with a free tier that includes an ad and tracking blocker. It is closed source, desktop only, and by default may use your content to improve the product unless you opt out.

products.name: Ungoogled Chromium

privacy.note: The project README says it removes all background requests to web services and blocks internal requests to Google at runtime, but that 'almost all' of its privacy tweaks 'must be manually activated', and it also disables Google Safe Browsing. It ships no tracker blocker turned on by default.

openness.note: Flathub's listing gives the build's licences as BSD-3-Clause plus the open-source licences of Chromium's components, and the project README says the code is BSD-3-clause.

portability.note: The README lists packages for many Linux distributions, Flathub, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and Homebrew on macOS, and the binaries page lists volunteer builds for Windows. There is no Google account sync and no mobile build.

respect.note: Ungoogled Chromium is a volunteer project that exists to remove Google web-service dependencies from Chromium, with no advertising, account or paid tier in the browser.

accessibility.note: The project FAQ says Chrome Web Store extensions can be installed only by a manual workaround, and 'There is currently no built-in functionality for auto-updates.' Its download page warns that binaries are submitted by volunteers and 'NOT official'.

economical.note: Homebrew lists Ungoogled Chromium as a free cask install for macOS; the browser has no price on any platform.

products.description: Chromium with every Google web-service connection stripped out, fully open source and run by volunteers. Most privacy settings are off until you change them, and there are no automatic updates or one-click extension installs.

products.name: Waterfox

privacy.note: Waterfox says its built-in desktop blocker prevents adverts, trackers, pop-ups and overlays from loading and 'This feature is enabled by default', and that the browser has 'no telemetry and no data collection'.

openness.note: Flathub lists Waterfox, published by BrowserWorks, under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and Waterfox describes itself as free and open source.

portability.note: Waterfox offers downloads for macOS, Windows and Linux and an Android app, and uses Firefox's Gecko engine so most Firefox extensions work. There is no iOS version.

respect.note: Waterfox's privacy policy says it adds a partner attribution parameter to searches on engines with which it has a revenue agreement, identifying the browser rather than the user, and runs its own search-suggestion proxy. Its homepage says it is funded through search partnerships, optional Waterfox Private Search subscriptions and donations, does not collect or sell personal data, and is owned by founder Alex Kontos's company BrowserWorks.

accessibility.note: Waterfox is a free download needing no account, built on the same engine as Firefox so most sites and extensions work, though it is an independently maintained browser with a much smaller support base.

economical.note: Waterfox says it is free with no premium tier or payment required.

products.description: An independent, open-source Firefox-based browser with ad and tracker blocking on by default and telemetry removed. It is funded largely by search partnerships, the same model Firefox relies on.

products.name: Floorp

privacy.note: Floorp's privacy policy says the desktop build disables Mozilla telemetry and health-report uploads by default, but some features still contact others, for example fetching missing site icons from Google's favicon service. Its tracking protection is the Firefox base it is built on rather than a separate blocker of its own.

openness.note: Flathub lists Floorp, published by Ablaze, under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and Floorp describes itself as an open source browser built on Firefox.

portability.note: Floorp is a free download for Windows, macOS and Linux with a built-in import tool and no account required; its iOS app is still in TestFlight testing.

respect.note: Floorp's privacy policy says the browser's desktop build turns off Mozilla telemetry, but the project's own website and blog run Google AdSense, including personalized ads.

accessibility.note: Floorp is a Firefox-based desktop browser with workspaces, split view and web panels; it is smaller and newer than Firefox, with mobile limited to an iOS test build.

economical.note: Floorp describes itself as a free, open source browser for Windows, macOS and Linux.

products.description: An open-source Firefox-based browser from a Japanese community project, built for heavy customization with workspaces and split view. It turns off Mozilla telemetry, though its own website carries Google ads.

products.name: Firefox Focus

privacy.note: Mozilla says Firefox Focus 'blocks a wide range of common trackers by default including social trackers', and lets a user erase history, passwords and cookies with one tap.

openness.note: The Firefox Focus for Android README in Mozilla's Firefox source tree describes it as an open source project under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

portability.note: Focus exists only for iOS and Android and is designed to keep nothing: Mozilla's Play listing describes it as having no recent history and no past sites, so there is nothing to sync or carry to another device.

respect.note: Focus is made by Mozilla, whose 2024 annual report says 'the majority of this revenue has come in the form of commercial search partnerships'. Google Play's data-safety listing says no data is shared with third parties.

accessibility.note: Focus is a free app with more than ten million Google Play downloads that opens straight to a search bar, but it has no extensions and keeps no history, so it suits quick private lookups rather than an everyday browser.

economical.note: Firefox Focus is free on iOS and Android.

products.description: Mozilla's minimal private browser for phones, blocking trackers by default and wiping everything with one tap. It is open source, but mobile only, with no extensions or history, so it works best as a second browser.

products.name: UC Browser

privacy.note: UC Browser's privacy policy, linked from ucweb.com and last updated April 2025, says it collects device information including the Android ID, usage, search and crash data, and network details, uses cookies to record 'what you search and view', and may share device and network information with AdMob by Google, Facebook Audience Network and Intowow. Google Play's data-safety listing still says 'Data isn’t encrypted'. Citizen Lab found in 2015 that the Android app leaked IMSI, IMEI, location and search queries over unencrypted or weakly encrypted connections.

openness.note: ucweb.com offers UC Browser only as a Windows installer and an Android app or APK, marked 'Copyright © 2025 UCWEB All rights reserved.', and publishes no browser source. In 2015 Citizen Lab had to analyse the app's network traffic from outside because no source was available.

portability.note: UC Browser is distributed as an Android app on Google Play and keeps browsing data inside its own app rather than a cross-platform sync service with an open export path.

respect.note: UC Browser's current privacy policy says the service is connected to the advertising platforms AdMob by Google, Facebook Audience Network and Intowow and may share device and network information with them, and Google Play flags that the app contains ads. In June 2020 India's Ministry of Electronics and IT blocked UC Browser as one of 59 apps it called 'prejudicial to sovereignty and integrity of India', citing citizen complaints about data security and privacy.

accessibility.note: Google Play lists UC Browser at more than one billion downloads and shows an October 2026 update, and ucweb.com now offers a Windows version too. India, which Citizen Lab named as one of its two biggest markets, blocked it in June 2020.

economical.note: UC Browser is free to download and is funded by ads, which Google Play flags.

products.description: A huge ad-supported mobile browser from Alibaba's UCWeb, now also on Windows. Its own privacy policy says it shares device and network data with ad networks, Google Play says its data is not encrypted, independent researchers found it leaking personal data in 2015 and India blocked it in 2020.

products.name: Yandex Browser

privacy.note: Yandex Browser's licence agreement says that with its statistics feature enabled, Yandex receives the websites visited, pages viewed, files downloaded and details of software installed on the device, and that Yandex 'has the right to use the said data in its other services and software for any purposes'. The mobile versions also send geolocation, SIM-card data and the list of installed apps. Users can switch the statistics feature off in settings.

openness.note: Yandex Browser's licence agreement forbids reproducing or distributing the software without the rightholder's written consent; it is a closed Yandex product.

portability.note: The licence agreement describes a Synchronization feature that stores settings, extensions, passwords, bookmarks and history on Yandex's servers so they follow a user between copies of the browser, which ties that data to Yandex.

respect.note: Yandex's privacy policy says personal information is used to personalize advertisements based on search history and other data. Yandex N.V. completed the sale of all its Russia-based businesses to an unnamed purchaser consortium in July 2024.

accessibility.note: Google Play lists Yandex Browser at more than 100 million downloads and flags that it contains ads; it is a mainstream choice mainly in markets where Yandex services are common.

economical.note: Yandex Browser is a free, ad-supported download.

products.description: A browser from Russia's Yandex whose own licence lets it collect browsing statistics and use them across its other services. It is free and widely installed where Yandex is popular, but closed and built around Yandex's advertising business.

products.name: Cromite

privacy.note: Cromite's README describes it as a Chromium fork based on Bromite 'with built-in support for ad blocking and an eye for privacy', aiming to disable features usable for tracking, while warning that its anti-fingerprinting is 'not comprehensive' and pointing at-risk users to Tor Browser.

openness.note: The README says Cromite is published under the GNU GPL v3, with Cromite-specific patches under GPL-2+.

portability.note: Cromite is built for Android 10 and above, Windows x64 and Linux, with no macOS or iOS version, and auto-updates have to be set up separately for each platform.

respect.note: Cromite is a volunteer project funded only by optional PayPal donations, with no advertising or account system in the browser.

accessibility.note: Cromite is distributed through its own repository and F-Droid repo rather than the major app stores, and its README walks users through manual auto-update setup on Windows and Linux.

economical.note: Cromite is free to download; donations are optional.

products.description: A volunteer-run, GPL-licensed Chromium fork that carries on Bromite's work, with built-in ad blocking and tracking features turned off. It runs on Android, Windows and Linux but is installed and updated outside the usual app stores.

products.name: GNOME Web (Epiphany)

privacy.note: The Arch Wiki says GNOME Web's ad blocking, using EasyList, is 'Enabled by default', and that WebKit's Intelligent Tracking Prevention is available in Preferences. GNOME's own archived privacy policy says Web 'enables Intelligent Tracking Prevention by default'.

openness.note: Flathub lists GNOME Web, published by The GNOME Project, under GPL-3.0 or later.

portability.note: GNOME Web is a Linux desktop browser built for GNOME. It can sync through Mozilla's Firefox Sync service, but there is no Windows, Mac or mobile version.

respect.note: GNOME's privacy policy, now on a retired wiki, says GNOME Web 'receives no funding from advertisers' and that browsing data stays on the user's computer unless Sync is turned on. The browser's app page asks users to donate to the GNOME Foundation.

accessibility.note: The Arch Wiki describes Web as the default browser for the GNOME desktop that also works in other Linux desktops, but it is Linux-only and uses the WebKit engine (GNOME's privacy policy points to WebKit's tracking-prevention documentation) rather than the Chromium or Firefox engines most sites are built against.

economical.note: GNOME Web is free software, offered at no charge with an optional donation link to the GNOME Foundation.

products.description: The GNOME desktop's own WebKit browser, free software with ad blocking on by default and no advertising funding. It runs only on Linux and its less common engine means some sites behave differently.

products.name: Opera GX

privacy.note: Opera GX advertises a built-in ad blocker and free browser VPN, but Opera's privacy statement says some of its applications 'serve targeted ads' based on IP address, a hashed user ID and general location, and GX's Google Play listing says it may share app performance data and device IDs with third parties.

openness.note: Opera GX is a proprietary Opera product, offered as a closed download for desktop and mobile rather than a published open-source browser.

portability.note: Opera's privacy statement says GX desktop runs on Windows and Mac, and the GX site says it is also available on iOS and Android, with Opera account sync for bookmarks and Speed Dial. There is no Linux version.

respect.note: Opera's privacy statement says it monetizes its free browsers 'primarily by selling advertising within the Applications themselves', alongside Cashback, AI shopping suggestions and paid GX Cloud content. Google Play flags that Opera GX contains ads.

accessibility.note: Opera GX is a free gaming-themed browser with more than 50 million Google Play downloads and built-in Discord, Twitch and messaging sidebars.

economical.note: Opera GX and its browser VPN are free; Opera sells a separate VPN Pro subscription and paid GX Cloud content.

products.description: Opera's gaming-themed browser, free and full of sidebar integrations, with a built-in ad blocker and VPN. Opera's own privacy statement says it earns money mainly by selling advertising inside its apps.
